source_text: Ἀλλὰ γὰρ ἐπανέλθωμεν εἰς τὴν τοῦ Ἰουδαίου προσωποποιΐαν, ἐν ᾗ ἀναγέγραπται ἡ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μήτηρ ὡς ἐξωσθεῖσα ὑπὸ τοῦ μνηστευσαμένου αὐτὴν τέκτονος, ἐλεγχθεῖσα ἐπὶ μοιχείᾳ καὶ τίκτουσα ἀπό τινος στρατιώτου Πανθήρα τοὔνομα· καὶ ἴδωμεν εἰ μὴ τυφλῶς οἱ μυθοποιήσαντες τὴν μοιχείαν τῆς παρθένου καὶ τοῦ Πανθήρα καὶ τὸν τέκτονα ἐξωσάμενον αὐτὴν ταῦτα πάντα ἀνέπλασαν ἐπὶ καθαιρέσει τῆς παραδόξου ἀπὸ ἁγίου πνεύματος συλλήψεως· ἐδύναντο γὰρ ἄλλως ψευδοποιῆσαι διὰ τὸ σφόδρα παράδοξον τὴν ἱστορίαν καὶ μὴ ὡσπερεὶ ἀκουσίως συγκαταθέσθαι ὅτι οὐκ ἀπὸ συνήθων ἀνθρώποις γάμων ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐγεννήθη. καὶ ἀκόλουθόν γε ἦν τοὺς μὴ συγκαταθεμένους τῇ παραδόξῳ γενέσει τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πλάσαι τι ψεῦδος· τὸ δὲ μὴ πιθανῶς αὐτοὺς τοῦτο ποιῆσαι ἀλλὰ μετὰ τοῦ τηρῆσαι ὅτι οὐκ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ παρθένος συνέλαβε τὸν Ἰησοῦν, τοῖς ἀκούειν καὶ ἐλέγχειν ἀναπλάσματα δυναμένοις ἐναργὲς ἦν ψεῦδος. ἆρα γὰρ εὔλογον τὸν τοσαῦτα ὑπὲρ τοῦ γένους τῶν ἀνθρώπων τολμήσαντα, ἵνα τὸ ὅσον ἐπ᾿ αὐτῷ πάντες Ἕλληνες καὶ βάρβαροι κρίσιν θείαν προσδοκήσαντες ἀποστῶσι μὲν τῆς κακίας πάντα δὲ πράττωσιν ἀρεσκόντως τῷ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργῷ, παράδοξον μὲν μὴ ἐσχηκέναι γένεσιν πασῶν δὲ γενέσεων παρανομωτάτην καὶ αἰσχίστην; ἐρῶ δὲ ὡς πρὸς Ἕλληνας καὶ μάλιστα Κέλσον, εἴτε φρονοῦντα εἴτε μὴ, πλὴν παρατιθέμενον τὰ Πλάτωνος· ἆρα ὁ καταπέμπων ψυχὰς εἰς ἀνθρώπων σώματα τὸν τοσαῦτα τολμήσοντα καὶ τοσούτους διδάξοντα καὶ ἀπὸ τῆς χύσεως τῆς κατὰ τὴν κακίαν μεταστήσοντα πολλοὺς ἀνθρώπων ἐπὶ τὴν πασῶν αἰσχροτέραν γένεσιν ὤθει, μηδὲ διὰ γάμων γνησίων αὐτὸν εἰσαγαγὼν εἰς τὸν τῶν ἀνθρώπων βίον; ἢ εὐλογώτερον ἑκάστην ψυχὴν κατά τινας ἀποῤῥήτους λόγους (λέγω δὲ ταῦτα νῦν κατὰ Πυθαγόραν καὶ Πλάτωνα καὶ Ἐμπεδοκλέα, οὓς πολλάκις ὠνόμασεν ὁ Κέλσος,) εἰσκρινομένην σώματι κατ᾿ ἀξίαν εἰσκρίνεσθαι καὶ κατὰ τὰ πρότερα ἤθη; εἰκὸς οὖν καὶ ταύτην τὴν ψυχὴν, πολλῶν (ἵνα μὴ συναρπάζειν δοκῶ, λέγων πάντων) ἀνθρώπων ὠφελιμωτέραν τῷ βίῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐπιδημοῦσαν, δεδεῆσθαι σώματος, οὐ μόνον ὡς ἐν ἀνθρωπίνοις σώμασι διαφέροντος ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῦ πάντων κρείττονος.
pass_a_gloss: But for let us return to the role of the Jew, in which it is written that the mother of Jesus, as having been sent away by the betrothed carpenter, having been convicted of adultery and bearing from a certain soldier Panthera by name; and let us see if not blindly those who fabricated the adultery of the virgin and Panthera and the carpenter having sent her away, all these things they fabricated for the purpose of abolishing the paradox of the conception from Holy Spirit; for they were able to fabricate falsehoods in another way because the story is very paradoxical and not as if unintentionally they agreed that Jesus was not born from the usual marriages of men; and it followed that those not agreeing with the paradoxical birth of Jesus would fabricate some falsehood; but that they did not do this plausibly but rather while keeping that the virgin did not conceive Jesus from Joseph, it was clear to those able to hear and examine fabrications that it was a falsehood; would it be reasonable then that the one who dared so much for the sake of the human race, so that all Greeks and barbarians, expecting divine judgment, would turn away from all wickedness and do all things pleasing to the creator of all, had a birth more lawless and shameful than all births? But I will say, as to Greeks and especially Celsus, whether he thinks or not, but setting forth the things of Plato; would the one who sends souls into human bodies have driven the one who dared so much and taught so many and changed many men from the flow of wickedness to the most shameful birth of all, not even introducing him into human life through genuine marriages? Or is it more reasonable that each soul, according to certain unspoken laws (I say these things now according to Pythagoras and Plato and Empedocles, whom Celsus often named), being judged worthy, is introduced into a body and judged according to former habits; it is likely then that this soul also, beneficial to the life of men, dwelling among men, was bound to a body, not only as one differing in human bodies but also of the one who is better than all.
pass_b_english: But let us return to the Jewish persona, in whose role it is written that Jesus’ mother was sent away by her betrothed, a carpenter, after being convicted of adultery and bearing a child by a certain soldier named Panthera. Let us see whether those who fabricated the story of the virgin’s adultery with Panthera and the carpenter’s rejection of her did so blindly, inventing all these details for the purpose of abolishing the paradox of a conception from the Holy Spirit. After all, they were able to fabricate falsehoods in another way precisely because the story is so extremely paradoxical, and they did not simply agree unintentionally that Jesus was not born from the usual marriages of men. It naturally followed that those who refused to accept the paradoxical birth of Jesus would fabricate some falsehood. Yet the fact that they did not do this plausibly—but instead maintained that the virgin did not conceive Jesus from Joseph—made it clear to anyone able to hear and examine fabrications that it was a lie. Would it be reasonable, then, that the one who dared so much for the sake of the human race—so that all Greeks and barbarians, expecting divine judgment, would turn away from wickedness and do all things pleasing to the Creator of all—should have had a birth more lawless and shameful than all other births? I will speak to Greeks and especially to Celsus, whether he is thoughtful or not, but setting forth Plato’s teachings. Would the one who sends souls into human bodies have driven the one who dared so much, taught so many, and turned many men from the flow of wickedness to the most shameful birth of all, without even introducing him into human life through genuine marriages? Or is it more reasonable that each soul, according to certain unspoken laws—I say this now according to Pythagoras, Plato, and Empedocles, whom Celsus often names—is judged worthy and introduced into a body according to its former habits? It is likely, then, that this soul also, more beneficial to human life than many others (so that I may not seem to snatch at the claim by saying “all”), dwelling among men, was bound to a body—not only as one differing among human bodies but also as the one who is better than all.

anf_compare.notes: Drafted from source only; ANF not shown to drafter.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex syntax of the Greek, including the parenthetical qualification regarding 'all' (ἵνα μὴ συναρπάζειν δοκῶ, λέγων πάντων) which Pass A omitted but Pass B correctly included. The distinction between the 'Jewish persona' (προσωποποιΐαν) and the 'role' is handled well. All theological and philosophical nuances regarding the soul's descent and the paradox of the birth are preserved.
